title: 2-Step Agent: How a Bayesian Decision Maker Learns from AI-Decision Support
claim: Adding decision support changes the reasoning flow: the agent updates beliefs with the prediction before estimating effects, versus using only prior and data.
layout: 2 stacked panels split by dashed line, left-to-right, numbered steps 1-3
description: Two horizontal flow diagrams stacked and separated by a dashed line. The top row, 'Process with ML-DS', starts with a sick patient icon. An arrow carries patient data, and an ML-DS box (AI → Prediction) feeds into a grey 'Doctor's reasoning' box. Inside that box, the 'Doctor's prior' points to 'Update beliefs', which points to 'Treatment effect estimation'. An arrow then leads to a pill icon and a recovered patient with a green check. The bottom row, 'Process without ML-DS', has the same flow but omits the ML-DS box and the belief update: patient data and the doctor's prior go straight into treatment effect estimation. Green circled numbers 1, 2 and 3 mark the stages. A thinking doctor cartoon sits above each reasoning box. Cartoon icons, black boxes and arrows, and light grey containers dominate.
caption: The flow of the framework for a clinical use case, with and without ML-DS. A new patient arrives for treatment, and the patient's data (1), potentially with the output of ML-DS, is observed by the agent, e.g. a doctor. Next, the agent estimates the effect of treatment and makes a treatment decision (2). Without ML-DS, this estimation is influenced by the agent's priors and patient data. With ML-DS, the agent uses these plus the ML prediction to update their beliefs about the population in a Bayesian fashion. The treatment and the patient's attributes determine the outcome (3).
abstract: Prognostic predictions from ML models support human decision making in several fields, including high-stakes ones such as healthcare and the judiciary. Yet, we still lack a clear understanding of how decision makers learn from ML-based decision support (ML-DS). In this paper, we introduce a general computational framework, the 2-Step Agent, to capture how a prediction from an ML model can also be used as a source of useful information about the training data and the causal mechanism that generated it. Our framework models (i) how a prediction from an ML model affects the beliefs of a rational Bayesian agent, and (ii) how this change in beliefs affects the estimation of the causal effect, the downstream decision for a new observation, and the subsequent outcome. In addition to the framework itself, we make three contributions. First, for the multivariate linear-Gaussian setting, we derive a tractable solution for the Bayesian inference problem introduced, i.e. one in which the agent infers information about a population from an ML prediction. Second, we experimentally identify conditions under which ML-DS is beneficial compared to unassisted decision making. Third, we show that a single misaligned prior belief of the user can be sufficient for ML-DS to lead to worse downstream outcomes compared to no decision support even when the prognostic model is well-specified and the agent is perfectly rational. Hence, even under ideal conditions, ML-DS can do more harm than good.
